chapter: Post office, day job and quitting
title: Post office route, carnival season and the union
summary: Musicians working day jobs, his mail route, going less often to play and keeping his union membership.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: There's an old man that we interviewed, Mr. Boullier. Boullier, yeah. He was in the folks' office service for the years.
Yeah, at one time, yes he was. But now, a lot of those guys, uh, how they do it during the ball carnival season, I don't know how they do it.

They play from ten to two, and they're right on the job the next day. Well, I tell you, that's kind of tough. Yeah. And I had a whole lot of easy in the lobby was either. I'm on the parts of the post-truck, see? It used to be my route around, uh, Josephine Louise's house, Warren's house, and all those places. That was my route for about eight years, and he changed me, put me up above Calvin Edmund. Well, I admit I had it just as easy, but it was very nice on there because I could get plenty of weight musically, you know? And at that time, that's between forty-five and fifty-five. Well, let's say that's from fifteen to fifteen to six years ago. Yeah. That does make a difference in your life, you know? I mean, I was younger. Did you quit then about six years ago?
Well, I tell you, you know, I kept on playing every chance I'd get.

I wouldn't play too much. I mean, go out looking for jobs, somebody called me, asked me to play, I would play. But, uh, the Musicians Union would give me what they call a project. Once or twice a year, so they claim that you can help you to pay your dues, but I mean, I have to pay my dues. I still belong to the Musicians Union, because they got a $1,000 policy. I wouldn't turn that down.
Oh yeah, the president. There's a lot of fellows to keep that.
